ESE 1205 Study Pack

Thermodynamics for Energy Engineering. One-shot notes, then every shortlisted past-paper topic (2017-2023) with full answers, slide figures and worked numericals. Your place, theme and text size are remembered on this device.

24-hour priority list

You answer 3 of 4 questions in each part, so each part has its own list. Study down both lists until the green pass line: about 5 h for Part A and 4 h for Part B, which leaves time for sleep and a last read of the one-shot notes. Alternate between parts (A block 1, B block 1, A block 2 …) so neither is left short. Chance: how often the topic came up, newer papers weigh more (2023 ×7, 2022 ×6, 2021 ×5, 2020 ×4, 2019 ×3, 2018 ×2, 2017 ×1). Covered: share of that part's past-paper marks you have studied once you finish the row.

Retake tip: read the Concept Primer for each block first (30 minutes), then follow this list. Psychrometry (B8) and gas mixtures (B7) are the biggest mark-earners in Part B and both have calculators; the Otto/Diesel numerical (B4) comes every year. In Part A the first law (A5, A6) and the second law (A7) are the safest. Entropy and exergy (A8, A9) are harder: do them last, using the calculators to practise.

★ One-shot notes

Every definition, formula and numerical recipe in one place. Read this first and again the night before.

One-shot notes: ESE 1205 Thermodynamics

Basic words (A1)

System / surroundings / boundary. Closed (control mass: energy only), open (control volume: mass + energy), isolated (nothing). Intensive (T, p, v) vs extensive (m, V, U); specific = extensive/m.

Equilibrium = Mechanical + Thermal + Chemical + Phase. Quasi-equilibrium = infinitely slow, can be drawn as a line. Cycle: ∮d(property) = 0. Steady: nothing inside changes with time.

Energy, heat, work (A2)

Stored E = KE + PE + U (sensible, latent, chemical, nuclear). In transit: Q (because of ΔT) and W (anything else), plus energy with mass flow.

Q, W are path functions (δQ, area under p-V), boundary phenomena. Heat or work depends on where you draw the boundary (oven example).

Pure substance (A3)

Fixed uniform composition. Water + steam = pure; liquid air + gas air = not pure (O2 condenses first). Phase rule F = C − π + 2. State postulate: 2 independent intensive properties.

x = (v − vf)/(vg − vf); v = vf + x vfg (same for u, h, s). Rigid tank = constant v: vertical line on T-v; Q = m(u2 − u1).

Gases (A4)

Pv = RT, R = 8.314/M. Z = Pv/RT; corresponding states: Z = f(PR, TR). Ideal if P << Pcr or T > 2Tcr.

vdW (P + a/v2)(v − b) = RT, a = 27R2Tcr2/64Pcr, b = RTcr/8Pcr. RK: 0.42748, 0.08664, √T. N2 175 K: ideal 13.85, vdW 9.47, RK 10.09 MPa (true 10).

First law (A5)

0th law → T; 1st → U; 2nd → S. Cycle: ∮δQ = ∮δW. Closed: Q − W = ΔU + ΔKE + ΔPE.

CV: dE/dt = Q̇ − Ẇ + Σṁ(h + V2/2 + gz)in − Σṁ(...)out. SFEE: q − w = Δh + ΔV2/2 + gΔz. Flow work pv ⇒ h = u + pv.

Wb: pVn → (p2V2 − p1V1)/(1 − n); n = 1 → p1V1ln(V2/V1); p const → pΔV.

Devices (A6)

Turbine w = h1 − h2; compressor/pump win = h2 − h1; pump w = vΔp; heat exchanger ṁhΔhh = ṁcΔhc; throttle h1 = h2; ṁ = AV/v. KE in kJ/kg = V2/2000.

Key answers: compressor 119.5 kW; pump 25.8 kW, steam 0.0616 kg/s; 2-stage turbine 17.36 kg/s, 17.6 MW, 3.82 MW; turbine 2023: 872.5 kJ/kg, 5.73 kg/s.

Second law (A7)

KP: no cycle produces work from a single reservoir. Clausius: no cycle moves heat cold → hot with no other effect. Equivalent (KP violator + fridge = Clausius violator).

Carnot principles: ηirr < ηrev; all reversible engines equal. (QL/QH)rev = TL/TH; ηC = 1 − TL/TH. Proof pattern: assume opposite → reverse the reversible one → one reservoir gives work.

Entropy (A8)

Clausius inequality ∮δQ/T ≤ 0 ⇒ dS = (δQ/T)rev. S2 − S1 = ∫δQ/T + Sgen; ΔSisolated ≥ 0.

T ds = du + p dv; T ds = dh − v dp. Ideal gas: Δs = cvln(T2/T1) + R ln(v2/v1) = cpln(v2/v1) + cvln(p2/p1). Solid/liquid: c ln(T2/T1).

CV: dS/dt = ΣQ̇/T + Σṁsin − Σṁsout + σ̇. ηC = (h2s − h1)/(h2a − h1); ηT = (h1 − h2a)/(h1 − h2s).

Exergy (A9) and relations (A10)

X = (U − U0) + p0(V − V0) − T0(S − S0) + KE + PE. Flow ψ = (h − h0) − T0(s − s0) + V2/2 + gz. Xdest = T0Sgen ≥ 0 (cannot create exergy). Wu = W − p0ΔV; ηII = Wu/Wrev.

Maxwell: (∂s/∂v)T = (∂p/∂T)v, (∂s/∂p)T = −(∂v/∂T)p, (∂T/∂v)s = −(∂p/∂s)v, (∂T/∂p)s = (∂v/∂s)p. β = (1/v)(∂v/∂T)p, κ = −(1/v)(∂v/∂p)T. Throttling cools only below max inversion T (μJT > 0).

Cycles basics (B1)

Air-standard: air ideal gas in closed loop, reversible, combustion → heat in, exhaust → heat out; cold-air: cp 1.005, cv 0.718, γ 1.4.

Carnot vapour cycle impractical: TH < 374 °C, wet turbine, two-phase compression. η = 1 − T0/Tm, Tm = (h3 − h2)/(s3 − s2).

Rankine (B2, B3)

1-2 pump, 2-3 boiler, 3-4 turbine, 4-1 condenser. η = [(h3 − h4) − v1Δp]/(h3 − h2). Improve: lower pcond, superheat, higher pboiler, reheat (pRH ≈ ¼-⅕ pB), regeneration.

Open FWH y = (h3 − h2)/(h6 − h2); η = 1 − (1 − y)(h7 − h1)/(h5 − h4).

Answers: 4 MPa/400 °C/27 °C: 38.2 % (actual 32.4 %); 3 MPa/355 °C/11 kPa: 33.2 %; reheat 15 MPa: pRH 4 MPa, 45.0 %; FWH 600 °C: y 0.227, 46.3 %; 550 °C: y 0.234, 45.5 %.

IC engines (B4)

Otto η = 1 − 1/rγ−1. Diesel η = 1 − (1/rγ−1)(rcγ − 1)/[γ(rc − 1)]. Dual: (rprcγ − 1)/[(rp − 1) + γrp(rc − 1)].

Same r: Otto > Dual > Diesel; same pmax: reverse. Diesel uses higher r (air only, no knock). MEP = wnet/(v1 − v2).

Answers: Otto r 4.89, 47 %; Diesel r 17: rc 1.95, 867 kJ/kg, 62.6 %; r 16: 2.01, 884, 61.3 %, MEP 699 kPa; Dual 2019 57.3 %; 2018 62.7 %.

Brayton (B5) and refrigeration (B6)

η = 1 − 1/rp0.2857; rbw = wc/wt. rp 8: 543 K, 718 K, 44.8 %; with 80/85 %: 604 K, 805 K, 0.615, 27.4 %; rp 5: 36.9 %, 176, 444.5 kJ/kg.

VCR: compressor → condenser → valve (h const) → evaporator; COP = (h1 − h4)/(h2 − h1). VAR: absorber + pump + generator replace compressor; heat-operated, quiet, low COP. Ice plant: 48.5 kW, motor 21.5 kW.

Gas mixtures (B7)

pi = yip (Dalton), Vi = yiV (Amagat). Mm = ΣyiMi = m/n; Rm = 8.314/Mm; cp = Σmficp,i, cp,i = γR/(γ − 1).

3 kg N2 + 5 kg CO2: y 0.485/0.515, M 36.24, R 0.2294, V 1.794 m3, ρ 4.46, cp 0.915, cv 0.686. 3.5 + 5.5 kg: y 0.5, M 36, V 3.28, cp 0.918.

Psychrometry (B8)

ω = 0.622pv/(p − pv); φ = pv/ps; μ = ω/ωs; φ = μ/[1 − (1 − μ)ps/p]; DPT = Tsat(pv); h = 1.005t + ω(2500 + 1.88t).

Carrier: pv = pwb − (p − pwb)(td − tw)/(1544 − 1.44tw). Adiabatic saturation: h const. DBT > WBT (evaporation cools the wick). Humid summer ⇒ slow drying, sweaty.

35/31: 0.0424 bar, 0.0272, 75.3 %, 30 °C, 104.9 kJ/kg. 30/27: 0.0337, 0.0214, 79.4 %, 26 °C.

UNDERSTAND Read this to understand; you do not need to write it

First law for a closed system: Q − W = ΔU (heat in minus work out = rise in stored energy). Boundary work is the area under the process on a p-V diagram, W = ∫p dV.

Interactive calculator (needs JavaScript; open the HTML version).

Before you start: the first law in one line

Energy cannot be created or destroyed. For any system: energy in − energy out = change of energy stored. For a closed system that becomes Q − W = ΔU + ΔKE (kinetic energy) + ΔPE (potential energy). For a device with flow (open system) we add the energy carried in and out by the flowing mass, which gives the steady-flow energy equation.

Enthalpy h = u + pv appears in open systems because the flow work pv (the work needed to push mass in or out) always comes with the internal energy u of the flowing mass.

Zeroth law (2019 2a, 2022 1a)

"If two bodies are each in thermal equilibrium with a third body, they are in thermal equilibrium with each other." Example: a thermometer (third body) reads 30 °C in a cup of water A and 30 °C in water B; so A and B, when brought into contact, exchange no heat. Property based on it: temperature; it is the basis of every thermometer.

Properties from the laws (2020 2b): zeroth law → temperature; first law → internal energy (and energy); second law → entropy.

First law statements and mathematical forms
  • For a cycle: "When a system undergoes a cycle, the net heat transfer equals the net work transfer": ∮δQ = ∮δW.
  • For a process of a control mass (closed system): Q − W = ΔE = ΔU + ΔKE + ΔPE; per unit time dE/dt = Q̇ − Ẇ.
  • For a control volume (open system), rate form:

dECV (control volume)/dt = Q̇CV − ẆCV + Σṁi(hi + Vi2/2 + gzi) − Σṁe(he + Ve2/2 + gze)

TermMeaning (unit kW)
dECV/dtrate of change of energy stored inside the control volume (zero at steady state)
Q̇CVnet rate of heat transfer into the CV across its boundary
ẆCVnet rate of work done by the CV other than flow work (shaft, electrical, moving boundary)
ṁi, ṁemass flow rates at inlets and exits (kg/s)
h = u + pventhalpy = internal energy + flow work per kg
V2/2, gzkinetic and potential energy per kg of the flowing stream (divide by 1000 to get kJ/kg)

Mass rate balance: dmCV/dt = Σṁi − Σṁe; at steady state Σṁi = Σṁe; with ṁ = ρAV = AV/v.

Derivation for an open system with one inlet and one exit (2022 2b, 15 marks)
Step (write this)Why / what it means
Take a control mass = CV contents at time t plus the small mass Δmi about to enter. At t + Δt it is the CV contents plus Δme that has just left.Trick: the first law is known for a fixed mass, so follow a fixed mass that passes through the CV.
Control mass first law: Q − W = E(t+Δt) − E(t)Apply Q − W = ΔE to that fixed mass.
E(t) = ECV(t) + Δmi(ui + Vi2/2 + gzi); E(t+Δt) = ECV(t+Δt) + Δme(ue + Ve2/2 + gze)Energy of the control mass at the two instants.
W = WCV + peveΔme − piviΔmiWork of the control mass = useful work of the CV + flow work: at the exit the mass pushes the surroundings (pA × distance = p × volume = p v Δm), at the inlet the surroundings push it in.
ECV(t+Δt) − ECV(t) = Q − WCV + Δmi(ui + pivi + Vi2/2 + gzi) − Δme(ue + peve + Ve2/2 + gze)Substitute and collect terms.
Divide by Δt, let Δt → 0, put h = u + pv:Rates: Δm/Δt → ṁ, Q/Δt → Q̇.
dECV/dt = Q̇CV − ẆCV + ṁi(hi + Vi2/2 + gzi) − ṁe(he + Ve2/2 + gze)The control-volume energy rate balance.
Steady flow (dECV/dt = 0, ṁi = ṁe = ṁ): q − w = (h2 − h1) + (V22 − V12)/2 + g(z2 − z1)The SFEE (steady-flow energy equation) asked in 2023 2b: per kg of fluid, q = Q̇/ṁ, w = Ẇ/ṁ.
Boundary work numericals
Before you start: boundary (p dV) work

When a piston moves, the gas does work W = ∫p dV (area under the p-V curve). Polytropic process pVn = C: W = (p2V2 − p1V1)/(1 − n) for n ≠ 1; for n = 1 (isothermal ideal gas) W = p1V1ln(V2/V1); for constant pressure W = p(V2 − V1). Use kPa × m3 = kJ.

2018 1d: p1 = 300 kPa, V1 = 0.1, V2 = 0.2 m3.

Step (write this)Why / what it means
(i) n = 1.5: p2 = p1(V1/V2)1.5 = 300(0.5)1.5 = 106.1 kPapVn = const gives the final pressure.
W = (106.1 × 0.2 − 300 × 0.1)/(1 − 1.5) = (21.21 − 30)/(−0.5) = 17.6 kJPositive: work done by the gas (expansion).
(ii) n = 1: W = p1V1ln(V2/V1) = 300 × 0.1 × ln 2 = 20.8 kJIsothermal curve lies higher, so more area, more work.

2019 2b: 8 kg gas, pV1.2 = C, p1 = 1000 kPa, V1 = 1 m3, p2 = 5 kPa, Δu = −40 kJ/kg.

Step (write this)Why / what it means
V2 = V1(p1/p2)1/1.2 = 1 × 2000.833 = 82.7 m3Final volume from the process law.
W = (p2V2 − p1V1)/(1 − n) = (5 × 82.7 − 1000)/(−0.2) = 2932 kJExpansion work.
ΔU = mΔu = 8 × (−40) = −320 kJ
Q = ΔU + W = −320 + 2932 = +2612 kJFirst law. Positive ⇒ 2612 kJ of heat flows into the gas.

2020 2c: constant pressure 105 kPa, V: 0.3 → 0.15 m3, Q = −37.6 kJ.

Step (write this)Why / what it means
W = p(V2 − V1) = 105(0.15 − 0.3) = −15.75 kJFrictionless (quasi-equilibrium) compression at constant pressure; negative = work done on the gas.
ΔU = Q − W = −37.6 − (−15.75) = −21.85 kJInternal energy decreases by 21.85 kJ.

Memory trick: "Q minus W equals Delta E" for everything; for flow add "h, V-squared over 2, g z" at each port. Laws and properties: 0 → T, 1 → U, 2 → S.

LEARN IT FROM ZERO
Second law and Carnot, from zero

The first law says energy is conserved; it does not say which way things go. Heat flows from hot to cold by itself, never the reverse. The second law puts this into two statements: Kelvin-Planck (no engine can turn all the heat it takes in into work: some must be rejected to a cold sink) and Clausius (no device can move heat from cold to hot without work input). Break one and you break the other.

The best possible engine between a hot reservoir TH and a cold one TL is the reversible Carnot engine: η = 1 − TL/TH (kelvin!). A real engine is always less. The same reversible machine run backwards is a refrigerator (COP = TL/(TH − TL)) or heat pump (COP = TH/(TH − TL)).

Interactive calculator (needs JavaScript; open the HTML version).

Before you start: why a second law?

The first law says energy is conserved, but not which way processes go. Hot coffee cools in a room; it never heats up by taking energy from the cooler room, even though that would not violate the first law. The second law gives the direction of processes and says that heat can never be fully converted into work in a cycle.

Thermal reservoir: a body so large that it can give or take any amount of heat without its temperature changing (ocean, atmosphere, furnace). Source = high-temperature reservoir, sink = low-temperature reservoir.

Heat engine: characteristics and efficiency (2023 3a)
  1. receives heat from a high-temperature source (furnace, solar, nuclear);
  2. converts part of this heat to work (usually a rotating shaft);
  3. rejects the remaining heat to a low-temperature sink (atmosphere, river);
  4. operates on a cycle, using a working fluid.

ηth = Wnet,out/QH = (QH − QL)/QH = 1 − QL/QH

Because QL can never be zero, η < 1. Typical values: car engine 25-30 %, steam plant 35-45 %, combined cycle up to 60 %.

Statements of the second law (2017 3a, 2019 4a, 2021 3a, 2022 3a)
  • Kelvin-Planck: "It is impossible for any device that operates on a cycle to receive heat from a single reservoir and produce an equal amount of work." Mathematical form: for a cycle exchanging heat with a single reservoir, Wcycle ≤ 0 (= 0 if reversible); equivalently ηth < 100 %.
  • Clausius: "It is impossible to construct a device that operates in a cycle and produces no effect other than the transfer of heat from a lower-temperature body to a higher-temperature body." A refrigerator needs work input.
  • Entropy statement: "It is impossible for any process to occur that decreases the total entropy of an isolated system": ΔSisolated = Sgen ≥ 0.
Equivalence of the two statements (2022 3a)
Step (write this)Why / what it means
Suppose an engine violates Kelvin-Planck: it takes QH from the hot reservoir and produces W = QH.Assume the impossible and look at the consequence.
Use this W to drive an ordinary refrigerator that takes QL from the cold reservoir and delivers QL + QH to the hot reservoir.First law for the refrigerator.
Combined system: no net work; takes QL from cold and gives net (QL + QH) − QH = QL to hot.Draw a boundary around both devices.
This combined device violates Clausius. Hence a KP (Kelvin-Planck (statement)) violation implies a Clausius violation; the reverse argument works the same way (Clausius violator + ordinary engine ⇒ KP violator).So the two statements are equivalent.
Reversible and irreversible processes

A reversible process can be reversed without leaving any trace on the system or surroundings. All real processes are irreversible. Irreversibilities: friction, heat transfer across a finite temperature difference, unrestrained expansion, mixing of different fluids, electrical resistance, inelastic deformation, chemical reaction. An internally reversible process has no irreversibility inside the system; totally reversible has none inside or at the boundary.

Can a frictionless engine be 100 % efficient? (2022 4b) No. Even with no friction and no irreversibilities, a heat engine must reject heat to a sink to complete its cycle (Kelvin-Planck). The best it can do is the Carnot efficiency 1 − TL/TH, which is below 1 because TL > 0 K.

Carnot principles (corollaries)
  1. The efficiency of an irreversible heat engine is always less than that of a reversible one operating between the same two reservoirs.
  2. The efficiencies of all reversible heat engines operating between the same two reservoirs are the same.
Proof 1: ηirr < ηrev (2020 3a, 2022 3b)
Step (write this)Why / what it means
Assume the opposite: ηirr > ηrev. Both receive the same QH from the hot reservoir.Proof by contradiction.
Then Wirr > Wrev and QL′ = QH − Wirr < QL = QH − Wrev.First law for each engine.
Reverse the reversible engine: it becomes a refrigerator taking Wrev, absorbing QL from the sink and delivering QH to the source.Only a reversible engine can be reversed with all quantities simply changing sign.
Let the irreversible engine drive it. Combined: hot reservoir net exchange = 0; net work out = Wirr − Wrev > 0; heat taken from the sink = QL − QL′ > 0.Boundary around both devices and the hot reservoir.
The combination produces work while exchanging heat with a single reservoir (the sink): this violates Kelvin-Planck.Contradiction.
Therefore ηirr < ηrev.
Proof 2: all reversible engines between the same reservoirs have the same efficiency (2023 3b)
Step (write this)Why / what it means
Take two reversible engines R1 and R2 between TH and TL; suppose ηR1 > ηR2.
Run R2 backwards as a refrigerator, driven by R1; both exchange the same QH.Same set-up as proof 1, with R1 in place of the irreversible engine.
The combination gives net work WR1 − WR2 > 0 from the single low-temperature reservoir: violates Kelvin-Planck. So ηR1 > ηR2 is impossible.
Now suppose ηR2 > ηR1: reverse R1 instead (it is also reversible); same contradiction.This step is possible only because both are reversible.
Hence ηR1 = ηR2: the efficiency of a reversible engine depends only on the reservoir temperatures, ηrev = f(TH, TL).Conclusion; leads to the thermodynamic temperature scale.
Proof 3: (QL/QH)rev = TL/TH (2017 4a, 17 marks; 2018 4d)
Step (write this)Why / what it means
From proof 2: QH/QL = f(TH, TL) for any reversible engine.Assumption: reversible engines, reservoirs only.
Engine A works between T1 and T3; engine B between T1 and an intermediate T2; engine C between T2 and T3, using the heat B rejects. B + C together equal A.Three reservoirs T1 > T2 > T3.
Q1/Q3 = f(T1,T3), Q1/Q2 = f(T1,T2), Q2/Q3 = f(T2,T3)
Q1/Q3 = (Q1/Q2)(Q2/Q3) ⇒ f(T1,T3) = f(T1,T2) f(T2,T3)The left side does not contain T2, so T2 must cancel on the right.
So f(T1,T2) = φ(T1)/φ(T2) ⇒ QH/QL = φ(TH)/φ(TL)Only a ratio form satisfies the product rule.
Kelvin chose φ(T) = T (the thermodynamic, absolute scale): (QL/QH)rev = TL/THTemperatures must be absolute (K).
Carnot efficiency (2017 5b, 2019 4d)
Step (write this)Why / what it means
η = 1 − QL/QHDefinition for any engine.
Carnot engine is reversible ⇒ QL/QH = TL/THProof 3 (or: on T-s, QH = THΔs and QL = TLΔs for the isothermal processes).
ηCarnot = 1 − T2/T1 = (T1 − T2)/T1Highest possible efficiency between T1 and T2; increases if T1 rises or T2 falls.

Short notes (2019 4d): Carnot efficiency: maximum efficiency of any engine between two reservoirs, 1 − TL/TH. Irreversible process: cannot be reversed without leaving a change in the surroundings (friction, finite ΔT, mixing). Clausius inequality: ∮δQ/T ≤ 0 (see A8). Thermal reservoir: very large body that supplies or absorbs heat at constant temperature.

Memory trick: Kelvin-Planck = Kilowatts from one reservoir impossible (engine). Clausius = Cold to hot needs work (fridge). Carnot proofs always: "assume the opposite → reverse the reversible one → one reservoir gives work → KP violated".

UNDERSTAND Read this to understand; you do not need to write it

Steady-flow energy equation: Q̇ − Ẇ = ṁ[(h2 − h1) + (V2² − V1²)/2000 + g(z2 − z1)/1000]. Turbine: Ẇ positive. Compressor/pump: Ẇ negative. Nozzle: no W, KE rises. Throttle: h1 = h2.

Interactive calculator (needs JavaScript; open the HTML version).

Before you start: how to solve any device problem in five steps

1) Draw the device and the control volume; number the inlet and exit states. 2) Write what is known at each state (two properties each). 3) Get h from tables (steam) or h = cpT / air table (ideal gas). 4) Write the steady-flow energy equation Q̇ − Ẇ = ṁ[(h2 − h1) + (V22 − V12)/2 + g(z2 − z1)] and drop terms that are zero. 5) Solve, then check the sign makes sense.

Units: V2/2 in m2/s2 = J/kg, so divide by 1000 for kJ/kg. Heat lost by the device is negative Q̇; power absorbed by a compressor or pump comes out negative Ẇ.

Turbine (2017 2b): a rotary machine in which a fluid flowing through blades turns a shaft and produces work. Kinds used in power generation: steam turbine (impulse and reaction, thermal plants), gas turbine (Brayton cycle), hydraulic turbine (Pelton, Francis, Kaplan in hydro plants), wind turbine.

1. Air compressor (2017 2b, 2022 2c)
Step (write this)Why / what it means
ṁ = p1A1V1/(RT1) = 100 × 0.1 × 6/(0.287 × 290) = 0.721 kg/sMass flow from the inlet: ṁ = AV/v and v = RT/p.
h1 = 290.16, h2 = 451.80 kJ/kgIdeal-gas air table at 290 K and 450 K (constant cp gives 1.005 × 160 = 160.8, almost the same).
ΔKE = (22 − 62)/2/1000 = −0.016 kJ/kgTiny compared with Δh.
Q̇ = −180 kJ/min = −3.0 kWHeat leaves the compressor.
Ẇ = Q̇ − ṁ[(h2 − h1) + ΔKE] = −3.0 − 0.721(161.64 − 0.016)SFEE (steady-flow energy equation) solved for Ẇ; ΔPE = 0.
Ẇ = −119.5 kW (power input 119.5 kW)Negative sign = work done on the air.
Neglecting ΔKE: Ẇ = −3.0 − 0.721 × 161.64 = −119.5 kW (difference 0.01 kW)2022 part 2: KE change is negligible here.

Ẇp = Q̇ + ṁ[(h1 − h2) + g(z1 − z2)]SFEE, KE neglected.
= −2 + 50[(417.46 − 417.69) + 9.81(−25)/1000] = −2 + 50(−0.23 − 0.245)
Ẇp = −25.8 kW ⇒ pump needs 25.8 kW(i) Answer.
Turbine CV: h3 (30 bar, 400 °C) = 3230.9; h4 (5 bar, 180 °C) = 2812.0 kJ/kgSuperheated steam table.
Turbine drives the pump: Ẇt = 25.8 kW = ṁs(h3 − h4)Adiabatic turbine, KE and PE negligible; all its power goes to the pump.
ṁs = 25.8/(3230.9 − 2812.0) = 0.0616 kg/s(ii) Answer.

Recommendation: the system recovers 13 kW (about 19 % of the 67.7 kW available). It is worth installing only if its capital, maintenance and operating cost can be paid back from about Tk 0.7 million per year; for a small turbine-generator set that is usually feasible within a few years, so it is recommended if the oven runs continuously. State this conclusion with the assumption about operating hours.

★ REMEMBER IT
  • Quality x = mass of vapour / total mass (only inside the dome). Any property: y = yf + x yfg. Phase rule: F = C − P + 2 (pure water at the triple point: F = 1 − 3 + 2 = 0).
Before you start: pure substance, phases and the steam tables

Most energy machines use water and steam. Water can be liquid, a liquid-vapour mixture, or vapour. To find its properties (v, u, h, s) we use steam tables, and to use them we must know which region we are in. The T-v diagram is the map of those regions.

Key words: saturation temperature = boiling temperature at a given pressure (100 °C at 101.325 kPa, 212 °C at 2 MPa). Quality x = fraction of the mixture mass that is vapour (0 for saturated liquid, 1 for saturated vapour).

Pure substance and phase

Pure substance: a substance with a fixed and uniform chemical composition throughout. It may be a single element or compound (water, N2, CO2) or a mixture, provided the mixture is homogeneous and its composition does not change (dry air as a gas). Phase: a quantity of matter that is homogeneous in chemical composition and physical structure (solid, liquid, gas), separated from other phases by a boundary.

Which mixture is a pure substance? (2020 1c, 2023 1a)

  1. Liquid water + water vapour: a pure substance. Both phases have the same chemical composition (H2O), so the composition is uniform even though two phases exist.
  2. Liquid air + gaseous air: NOT a pure substance. Air is mainly N2 and O2, which condense at different temperatures (O2 at −183 °C, N2 at −196 °C). So the liquid is richer in oxygen and the vapour richer in nitrogen; composition differs between phases.

When can air be treated as a pure substance? (2019 1b) As long as it stays entirely in one phase (all gas, at ordinary temperatures), so its composition is the same everywhere and does not change. Once condensation starts, it is no longer pure.

Gibbs phase rule (non-reacting system)

F = C − π + 2

  • F = degrees of freedom = number of independent intensive properties that must be fixed to fix the state.
  • C = number of chemical components (distinct species).
  • π = number of phases present.
  • Water, one phase (superheated steam): F = 1 − 1 + 2 = 2 (need p and T). Water + steam: F = 1 − 2 + 2 = 1 (fix p and T is fixed automatically). Triple point: F = 1 − 3 + 2 = 0 (unique p and T).
State postulate (2017 1c, 2019 4b, 2023 1b)

"The state of a simple compressible system is completely specified by two independent, intensive properties." A simple compressible system is one in which electrical, magnetic, gravitational, motion and surface-tension effects are absent.

Significance: (i) we only need two properties (e.g. p and T) to look up all the others in a table, which is how every steam-table problem works; (ii) the two must be independent: inside the wet region p and T are not independent (T = Tsat(p)), so we need p and x, or T and v, etc.; (iii) it allows property diagrams in two coordinates (T-v, p-v, T-s, h-s).

T-v diagram of a pure substance (2018 2a, 2023 2a)
  • Saturated liquid line (left side of dome) and saturated vapour line (right side) meet at the critical point (water: 22.06 MPa, 373.95 °C, v = 0.003106 m3/kg).
  • Regions: compressed (subcooled) liquid left of the dome; saturated liquid-vapour (wet) mixture under the dome; superheated vapour right of the dome.
  • A constant-pressure line rises in the liquid region, runs horizontal across the dome (T = Tsat), then rises again in the superheated region. Higher pressures lie higher. Constant-quality lines fan out inside the dome from the critical point (x = 0.25, 0.5, 0.75).
Quality and the derivation x = (v − vf)/(vg − vf) (2017 1c)
Step (write this)Why / what it means
x = mg/mt, mt = mf + mgDefinition: g = saturated vapour, f = saturated liquid, t = total.
V = Vf + Vg ⇒ mtv = mfvf + mgvgVolumes add; each volume = mass × specific volume.
mf = mt − mg ⇒ v = (1 − x)vf + x vgDivide by mt and use mg/mt = x.
v = vf + x(vg − vf) = vf + x vfgRearrange.
x = (v − vf)/(vg − vf)Quality = how far along the horizontal line the state lies (lever rule). Same form for u, h, s.
Numerical: rigid tank cooled (2019 1d, 10 marks)

Given: rigid tank, water, p1 = 2 MPa, x1 = 0.8, V = 0.5 m3; cooled to p2 = 0.4 MPa. Find: Q.

Step (write this)Why / what it means
At 2 MPa: vf = 0.001177, vg = 0.09959 m3/kg; uf = 906.12, ufg = 1693.0 kJ/kgSaturated-water pressure table at 2 MPa (Tsat = 212.4 °C).
v1 = 0.001177 + 0.8(0.09959 − 0.001177) = 0.07990 m3/kgSpecific volume of the wet mixture.
m = V/v1 = 0.5/0.07990 = 6.26 kgMass in the tank (stays constant: closed system).
u1 = 906.12 + 0.8 × 1693.0 = 2260.5 kJ/kgInternal energy at state 1.
v2 = v1 = 0.07990 (rigid)Rigid tank: volume and mass fixed ⇒ v fixed. This is the second property that fixes state 2.
At 0.4 MPa: vf = 0.001084, vg = 0.4624; uf = 604.22, ufg = 1948.9Pressure table at 0.4 MPa (143.6 °C). v2 lies between vf and vg, so still wet.
x2 = (0.07990 − 0.001084)/(0.4624 − 0.001084) = 0.171Quality after cooling: most of the vapour has condensed.
u2 = 604.22 + 0.171 × 1948.9 = 937.2 kJ/kg
Q = m(u2 − u1) = 6.26(937.2 − 2260.5)First law, closed rigid system: W = 0 (no boundary movement), ΔKE (kinetic energy) = ΔPE (potential energy) = 0.
Q = −8281 kJ ≈ −8.28 MJNegative ⇒ 8.28 MJ of heat leaves the water.

Memory trick: "Two to tango": two independent intensive properties fix a state. Phase rule "F = C − P + 2" = "Freedom = Components minus Phases plus 2". Rigid tank = vertical line on T-v.

LEARN IT FROM ZERO
Exergy, from zero

Exergy = the useful work you could still get from something before it becomes just like its surroundings (the dead state, T0 = 25 °C, p0 = 1 atm). A tank of compressed air at room temperature has no extra heat, but it can still push a turbine: it has exergy. Hot coffee has exergy; the same energy spread through the room has none.

Closed system: φ = (u − u0) + p0(v − v0) − T0(s − s0) + V²/2 + gz. Flowing stream: ψ = (h − h0) − T0(s − s0) + V²/2 + gz. Exergy destroyed = T0Sgen. Second-law efficiency = actual work / reversible work.

Interactive calculator (needs JavaScript; open the HTML version).

Before you start: exergy = the useful part of energy

Energy is conserved, but its quality is not. 1000 kJ in a furnace at 1500 K can produce much more work than 1000 kJ in warm water at 40 °C. Exergy (availability) is the maximum useful work that can be obtained from a system as it is brought to equilibrium with the environment.

Dead state: the state of the system when it is in complete equilibrium with the environment (T0 = 25 °C, p0 = 1 atm, at rest, at zero elevation, no chemical difference). At the dead state the exergy is zero.

Definitions
  • Exergy: maximum useful work obtainable from a system at a given state in a given environment (when it is taken reversibly to the dead state).
  • Useful work vs actual work (2021 4a): Wu = W − Wsurr = W − p0(V2 − V1). When a system expands it must push back the atmosphere; that part p0ΔV is not available for any useful purpose.
  • Reversible work Wrev: maximum useful work between two states; irreversibility I = Xdestroyed = Wrev − Wu = T0Sgen.
  • Second-law efficiency ηII = Wu/Wrev (work-producing) or Wrev/Wu (work-consuming) = exergy recovered/exergy expended.

Is it possible to generate exergy? (2020 3b) No. Every real process destroys exergy (Xdestroyed = T0Sgen ≥ 0) because Sgen ≥ 0 by the second law. A reversible process at best conserves it. So exergy can only be transferred or destroyed, never created (unlike energy, which is always conserved).

Physical significance (2022 4c): exergy tells the true potential of an energy source; it locates and measures losses (where exergy is destroyed: combustion, heat transfer across large ΔT, throttling) and so shows where improvement is possible; it allows fair comparison of systems through ηII.

Derivation: exergy of a closed system (2017 4b, 2018 4a, 2019 4c, 2021 4a)
Step (write this)Why / what it means
Let the system (U, V, S, KE, PE) go to the dead state while exchanging heat δQ only with the environment at T0; to make it reversible, the heat passes through a reversible heat engine.Combined system = closed system + reversible engine.
Closed system first law: −δQ − δW = dU (here δQ = heat leaving the system)Energy balance.
δW = p dV + δWb,useful... write δW = p0dV + δWb,uBoundary work = work against the atmosphere + useful boundary work.
Reversible engine: δWHE = δQ(1 − T0/T) = δQ − T0δQ/T = δQ − T0(−dS)Carnot efficiency of the tiny engine; δQ/T = −dS for the system (reversible heat leaving).
Total useful work: δWtotal,u = δWHE + δWb,u = −dU − p0dV + T0dSAdd and use the first-law relation to remove δQ.
Integrate from the given state to the dead state (0): Wtotal,u = (U − U0) + p0(V − V0) − T0(S − S0)
Add the kinetic and potential energies, which are fully convertible to work:They are mechanical energy, 100 % exergy.
X = (U − U0) + p0(V − V0) − T0(S − S0) + KE + PEThis maximum work = exergy Wc of the closed system. Per kg: φ = (u − u0) + p0(v − v0) − T0(s − s0) + V2/2 + gz.
Derivation: exergy of a flow stream (2023 4c)
Step (write this)Why / what it means
A flowing fluid carries flow work pv per kg; of this, p0v must be spent pushing the atmosphere, so the useful flow work is (p − p0)v.Flow exergy = closed exergy + exergy of flow work.
ψ = φ + (p − p0)vAdd the useful flow work to the fluid's non-flow exergy.
= (u − u0) + p0(v − v0) − T0(s − s0) + V2/2 + gz + pv − p0v
= (u + pv) − (u0 + p0v0) − T0(s − s0) + V2/2 + gzThe p0v terms cancel.
ψ = (h − h0) − T0(s − s0) + V2/2 + gzh = u + pv.

dXCV (control volume)/dt = Σ(1 − T0/Tk)Q̇k − (Ẇ − p0dVCV/dt) + Σṁiψi − Σṁeψe − Ẋdestroyed

Terms: rate of change of exergy in the CV; exergy transfer with heat at boundary temperature Tk (heat is worth only its Carnot fraction); exergy transfer with useful work; exergy carried in and out by mass (flow exergy ψ); exergy destroyed Ẋdestroyed = T0Ṡgen ≥ 0.

LEARN IT FROM ZERO
Entropy, from zero

Entropy is the second law turned into a property. Think of it as a measure of spread-out-ness of energy. When heat Q enters at temperature T, entropy rises by Q/T. Friction, mixing and heat flowing across a temperature gap create extra entropy (Sgen > 0) that can never be destroyed. So: ΔS = ∫δQ/T + Sgen, with Sgen = 0 only for a perfect (reversible) process.

An isentropic process (adiabatic and reversible) is the ideal turbine or compressor. Real machines are compared with it: compressor η = ws/wa, turbine η = wa/ws (the ideal one is always the better one, so it goes on top for the compressor and at the bottom for the turbine).

Interactive calculator (needs JavaScript; open the HTML version).

Before you start: what entropy is

Entropy S (kJ/K) is a property that measures molecular disorder and, in engineering, the loss of the ability to do work. Heat added to a system raises its entropy; friction and other irreversibilities generate entropy. It is defined through reversible heat transfer: dS = (δQ/T)int rev.

Practical meaning: an isentropic (s = constant) process is the ideal, loss-free adiabatic process. Real turbines and compressors are compared with it through the isentropic efficiency.

Clausius inequality and dS = (δQ/T)int rev (2017 3b, 2018 3c, 2021 3b)

∮ (δQ/T)b ≤ 0 ( = 0 for an internally reversible cycle, < 0 for an irreversible cycle)

Step (write this)Why / what it means
Consider a system receiving δQ at boundary temperature T, combined with a reversible cyclic device that supplies this δQ from a reservoir at TR.Standard Clausius set-up.
For the reversible device: δQR/TR = δQ/T. Combined work δWC = TR(δQ/T) − dEC.Proof 3 of A7 gives Q ratio = T ratio for a reversible device.
Over a full cycle of the system: WC = TR∮δQ/T (since ∮dE = 0).
The combination exchanges heat with one reservoir only, so by Kelvin-Planck WC ≤ 0 ⇒ ∮δQ/T ≤ 0.TR > 0.
For an internally reversible cycle the inequality must be equality (reverse it and the sign flips): ∮(δQ/T)int rev = 0.
A quantity whose cyclic integral is zero depends only on the state: it is a property. Call it entropy: dS = (δQ/T)int rev.Same logic as volume: ∮dV = 0.

Reversible process (2018 3c): a process that can be reversed leaving no change in either system or surroundings; it has no friction, no finite-ΔT heat transfer, no unrestrained expansion or mixing.

Increase of entropy principle (2022 3d)

For any process 1-2: S2 − S1 ≥ ∫δQ/T, i.e. S2 − S1 = ∫δQ/T + Sgen, with Sgen ≥ 0. For an isolated system (or system + surroundings) δQ = 0, so ΔSisolated = Sgen ≥ 0. Entropy of the universe can increase or stay constant (reversible) but never decrease; processes go only in the direction that increases total entropy. Sgen = 0 reversible, > 0 irreversible, < 0 impossible.

Only work interaction (2020 2a): the system still contains entropy (every substance above 0 K has entropy). Work carries no entropy, so if the work is done reversibly (e.g. slow frictionless compression with no heat) its entropy does not change. If the work involves irreversibility (paddle-wheel stirring, friction) entropy is generated inside and S increases. It can never decrease by work alone.

Tds equations (asked in 5 papers)
Step (write this)Why / what it means
Closed simple compressible system, internally reversible process: δQint rev − δWint rev = dUFirst law in differential form.
δQint rev = T dS (definition of entropy); δWint rev = p dV (boundary work)
T dS = dU + p dV, per kg T ds = du + p dv — first Tds (Gibbs) equationRelates only properties, so it holds for ANY process (reversible or not) between the same states.
h = u + pv ⇒ dh = du + p dv + v dp ⇒ du + p dv = dh − v dp
T ds = dh − v dp — second Tds equation

Incompressible substance (2019 3b): dv = 0 and du = c dT, so ds = du/T = c(T)dT/T and s2 − s1 = ∫T1T2 c(T)dT/T ≈ cavgln(T2/T1).

Ideal gas (2022 4a): derive s2 − s1 = cpln(v2/v1) + cvln(p2/p1).

Step (write this)Why / what it means
ds = du/T + (p/T)dv = cvdT/T + R dv/vFirst Tds; ideal gas du = cvdT and p/T = R/v.
s2 − s1 = cvln(T2/T1) + R ln(v2/v1)Integrate with constant cv.
T2/T1 = p2v2/(p1v1) ⇒ ln(T2/T1) = ln(p2/p1) + ln(v2/v1)From pv = RT at both states.
s2 − s1 = cvln(p2/p1) + (cv + R)ln(v2/v1)
s2 − s1 = cpln(v2/v1) + cvln(p2/p1)cv + R = cp. (Other forms: cpln(T2/T1) − R ln(p2/p1).)

TermMeaning (kW/K)

Q̇j/Tjentropy transfer with heat at the part of the boundary where the temperature is Tj
ṁisi, ṁeseentropy carried in and out by mass flow
σ̇CVrate of entropy production by irreversibilities inside (≥ 0)

★ REMEMBER IT
  • System types by what crosses the boundary: open (mass + energy), closed (energy only), isolated (nothing).
  • Intensive = does not depend on size (T, p, ρ); extensive = doubles when you double the system (m, V, E). Specific (per kg) properties are intensive.
Before you start: what thermodynamics talks about

Thermodynamics is the science of energy and its conversion from one form to another (heat into work in an engine, work into cooling in a fridge). Before any law can be applied we must say what we are studying: that chosen piece of the world is the system.

Everything in this topic is vocabulary. Learn each word with one example and one sketch; these short definitions are worth 5-10 marks in almost every paper.

System, surroundings, boundary and types of system

System: any quantity of matter or region of space chosen for study. Surroundings: everything outside it. Boundary: the real or imaginary surface separating the two; it may be fixed or moving.

TypeMass crosses boundary?Energy crosses boundary?Example
Closed system (control mass)NoYes (heat and work)Gas in a sealed piston-cylinder
Open system (control volume)YesYesTurbine, compressor, pump, nozzle, boiler
Isolated systemNoNoInsulated, rigid, sealed flask; the universe
Adiabatic system(either)No heat; work possibleWell-insulated turbine

Side note: "Control mass" = we follow a fixed lump of matter. "Control volume" = we watch a fixed region in space while matter flows through it. That is why the first-law equation for an open system has mass-flow terms.

Macroscopic and microscopic viewpoints (2018 1a, 2019 1a)
Macroscopic (classical) viewMicroscopic (statistical) view
Looks at the overall behaviour of the matter using a few measurable quantities: p, T, V, mLooks at the individual molecules: their positions, velocities and energies
Needs no model of molecular structureNeeds statistics and probability over a huge number of molecules
Valid when the system contains very many molecules (a continuum)Needed for rarefied gases (very few molecules) and to explain properties
Example: pressure of gas in a tyre read on a gaugeExample: the same pressure explained as the average force of molecules hitting the wall

Continuum (2021 1c): we ignore the gaps between molecules and treat matter as continuous, so that a property such as density has a definite value at every point (ρ = lim δm/δV as δV shrinks to a small but molecule-rich volume). It fails when the mean free path of molecules is comparable to the size of the system (high vacuum).

Property, state, and kinds of property
  • Property: any measurable characteristic of a system (p, T, V, m, U, H, S). Its value depends only on the state, not on how the system got there.
  • State: the condition of the system described by its properties at an instant.
  • Intensive property: independent of the size of the system: T, p, density, specific volume. If a block is cut in half, each half has the same T.
  • Extensive property: depends on size, is additive: m, V, U, H, S.
  • Specific property: extensive ÷ mass, e.g. v = V/m, u = U/m; it is intensive.
  • Internal property depends on the matter inside (u, h, s); external property does not depend on the nature of the matter: velocity V and elevation z of the system as a whole (2023 1c).
Thermodynamic equilibrium (2019 1c, 10 marks)

A system is in thermodynamic equilibrium when none of its properties change with time if it is isolated from the surroundings. It requires all of the following at once:

  1. Mechanical equilibrium: no unbalanced force inside the system or between it and the surroundings, so pressure is uniform (apart from gravity effects).
  2. Thermal equilibrium: no temperature difference within the system or with its surroundings across a diathermic wall.
  3. Chemical equilibrium: no chemical reaction and no transfer of a species from one part to another.
  4. Phase equilibrium: the mass of each phase stays constant (no net evaporation or condensation).

Only equilibrium states have single values of p, T, etc., so only they can be plotted on a property diagram and looked up in tables.

Process, path, cycle and quasi-equilibrium process
  • Process: any change from one equilibrium state to another. Path: the series of states passed through.
  • Quasi-equilibrium (quasi-static) process: carried out so slowly that the system stays infinitesimally close to equilibrium at every instant; it can be drawn as a solid line on a p-V diagram. A fast process is drawn dashed because intermediate states are not defined. Quasi-equilibrium processes are the ideal standard: they give the maximum work output from expanding devices and the minimum work input to compressors.
  • Cycle: a series of processes whose final state equals the initial state; every property returns to its initial value (∮dU = 0).
  • Iso-processes: isothermal (T const), isobaric (p const), isochoric (v const), isentropic (s const), adiabatic (Q = 0).
Steady vs transient analysis (2021 2b)
Steady state (steady flow)Transient (unsteady)
Properties at every point inside the control volume do not change with time: dmCV (control volume)/dt = 0, dECV/dt = 0Properties inside change with time
Mass in = mass out; energy in = energy outMass and energy stored in the CV change: min − mout = ΔmCV
Example: turbine, pump or heat exchanger running at constant loadExample: filling a gas cylinder, discharging a tank, starting up a turbine

Memory trick: Systems: C-O-I = Closed (only energy), Open (mass + energy), Isolated (nothing). Equilibrium: M-T-C-P = "My Tea Cools Properly": Mechanical, Thermal, Chemical, Phase.

A2 Energy: energy mind map, stored vs transient energy, heat vs work, path and point functions Likely · 75%Easy

Past-paper questions · Pass set

  • 2022 Q2(a) [10] "An energy transfer can be heat or work, depending on system selection": explain the statement.
  • 2021 Q1(a) [10] Why are heat and work path functions but thermodynamic properties point functions? Describe.
  • 2021 Q1(b) [10] Briefly explain the stored and transient forms of energy with the help of a schematic diagram.
  • 2020 Q1(d) [12] "An energy transfer can be heat or work, depending on system selection": explain the statement.
  • 2019 Q2(c) [12] Draw an energy mind map. Define the different terms in the map.
  • 2018 Q1(b) [10] Draw an energy mind map and describe each term in brief.
  • 2017 Q1(b) [10] Draw an energy mind map and describe each term in it.
★ REMEMBER IT
  • Heat and work are path functions (energy crossing the boundary, inexact differentials δQ, δW). Properties (p, T, U, H, S) are point functions (depend only on the state, exact dU).
Before you start: energy, heat and work in plain words

Energy is the capacity to cause change. A system can store energy (a moving car, a lifted weight, hot water) and energy can travel across the boundary of a system. When energy travels because of a temperature difference we call it heat (Q); when it travels for any other reason (a moving piston, a rotating shaft, an electric current) we call it work (W).

Units: kJ for energy, kW (= kJ/s) for rates. Sign convention used in the course: heat to the system is positive, work done by the system is positive.

Energy mind map (asked 2017, 2018, 2019: 10-12 marks)

Terms in the map:

  1. Stored energy E (property of the system) = macroscopic + microscopic energy: E = KE (kinetic energy) + PE (potential energy) + U.
  2. Kinetic energy KE = mV2/2: due to motion of the whole system relative to a reference frame.
  3. Potential energy PE = mgz: due to elevation of the whole system in a gravity field.
  4. Internal energy U: sum of all microscopic energies of the molecules: sensible (translation, rotation, vibration of molecules; shows up as temperature), latent (binding between molecules; released or absorbed during phase change), chemical (atomic bonds in molecules; released in combustion), nuclear (bonds inside the nucleus; released in fission/fusion).
  5. Energy in transit (not stored, exists only while crossing the boundary): heat by conduction, convection and radiation; work as boundary (p dV) work, shaft work, electrical work, flow work; and, for open systems, energy carried by mass flow.

Side note: A quick test: if you can say "the system has it", it is stored energy (a property). If you can only say "the system received or gave it", it is heat or work.

Stored and transient energy (2021 1b)

Stored forms are possessed by the system and are properties: KE, PE and U (with its sensible, latent, chemical and nuclear parts). Transient forms are recognised only as they cross the boundary: heat and work. Once inside, they become part of the stored energy; there is no "heat content" of a body. Sketch the mind map above with a dashed system boundary: arrows of Q and W cross the boundary, while KE, PE, U are written inside it.

Why heat and work are path functions and properties are point functions (2021 1a)
  • A point function (property) depends only on the state: going from state 1 to 2 by any path gives the same ΔV = V2 − V1. Its differential is exact (dV, dU), and ∮dV = 0 over a cycle.
  • Work W = ∫p dV is the area under the process curve on a p-V diagram. Different paths between the same states have different areas, so W depends on the path. Likewise Q depends on the path. Their small amounts are written δW, δQ (inexact differentials): ∫12δW = W12, never W2 − W1.
  • Heat and work are boundary phenomena: they exist only while crossing the boundary, so a system never "contains" heat or work and they cannot be properties.
"An energy transfer can be heat or work, depending on the system selection" (2020 1d, 2022 2a)

Example: an electric oven (or resistance heater) heating the air inside it.

  1. Boundary drawn around the air inside the oven only (heating element outside): the hot element is at a higher temperature than the air, so energy crosses the boundary because of a temperature difference: this is heat transfer.
  2. Boundary drawn around the whole oven including the heating element: electric current (electrons) crosses the boundary, which is electrical work, not heat; the energy content of the oven rises because of work done on it.
  3. Boundary drawn around oven + power supply (in the figure, generator driven by a falling weight): nothing crosses the boundary: Q = 0, W = 0; energy only changes form inside.

Therefore heat and work are not properties of the energy itself; they are labels for how the energy crosses a particular boundary. Always define the system first.

Memory trick: Heat needs ΔT at the wall; everything else is work. Mind map = "K-P-U stored, Q-W-M moving" (kinetic, potential, internal; heat, work, mass).

A4 Ideal gas and real gas: equations of state, compressibility factor Likely · 75%Medium

  • 2018 Q2(d) [5] What is compressibility factor? When a gas is modelled as an ideal gas, what are the equations to be used?

  • 2017 Q1(d) [11] What are the equations used when a gas is modelled as an ideal gas? 1 kg of air in a piston-cylinder undergoes a cycle: 1-2 constant specific volume, 2-3 constant temperature expansion, 3-1 constant pressure compression. At state 1, T = 300 K, p = 1.012 bar; at state 2, p = 2.0 bar. (i) Sketch the cycle on p-v, (ii) find T2, (iii) find v3 (M = 29).
  • 2017 Q4(c) [8] State the van der Waals equation of state and calculate the unknown constants in terms of critical pressure and temperature.
  • 2017 Q8(a) [5] Write down the comparison between ideal gases and real gases.
Before you start: ideal gas and why real gases deviate

An ideal gas is a model in which molecules occupy no volume and do not attract each other. Its equation of state is Pv = RT (or PV = mRT = nRuT). Ru = 8.314 kJ/kmol K is universal; R = Ru/M is the gas constant of a particular gas (air: 8.314/28.97 = 0.287 kJ/kg K).

Real molecules have size (volume b) and attraction (a). These matter when the gas is dense: high pressure, low temperature, near the saturation dome or the critical point. The compressibility factor Z = Pv/RT measures the deviation: Z = 1 for an ideal gas.

Equations used when a gas is modelled as an ideal gas (2017 1d, 2018 2d)
  • Pv = RT, PV = mRT, PV = nRuT, R = Ru/M, p1V1/T1 = p2V2/T2 (fixed mass).
  • u = u(T) and h = h(T) only: du = cvdT, dh = cpdT, cp − cv = R, γ = cp/cv.
  • Isentropic: pvγ = const, T2/T1 = (p2/p1)(γ−1)/γ = (v1/v2)γ−1.

When can a real gas be treated as ideal? (2021 4c) When its pressure is low compared with the critical pressure (PR = P/Pcr << 1) and/or its temperature is high compared with the critical temperature (TR > 2), i.e. far from the saturation dome; then Z ≈ 1. Air, N2, O2, H2 at room conditions qualify; steam in a boiler does not.

Compressibility factor and principle of corresponding states (2018 2d, 2022 1c)

Compressibility factor Z = Pv/(RT) = vactual/videal. Z = 1: ideal; Z < 1: attraction dominates (gas more compressible); Z > 1: molecular volume dominates.

Principle of corresponding states: when normalised by their critical properties (reduced pressure PR = P/Pcr, reduced temperature TR = T/Tcr), all gases have approximately the same Z. So one generalised compressibility chart works for every gas.

Ideal vs real gas (2017 8a)
Ideal gasReal gas
Obeys Pv = RT exactly, Z = 1Deviates, Z ≠ 1; needs vdW (van der Waals), RK (Redlich-Kwong), virial or Z-chart
Molecules have no volume, no intermolecular forcesMolecules have finite volume and attract each other
u, h depend on T onlyu, h depend on T and p
Never liquefiesLiquefies when cooled and compressed below Tcr
Good model at low p, high TMust be used at high p, low T, near saturation
van der Waals equation and its constants (2017 4c)

(P + a/v2)(v − b) = RT or P = RT/(v − b) − a/v2

a/v2 corrects for intermolecular attraction (it lowers the wall pressure); b corrects for the volume occupied by the molecules.

Step (write this)Why / what it means
At the critical point the isotherm has an inflection: (∂P/∂v)T = 0 and (∂2P/∂v2)T = 0Experimental fact: the Tcr isotherm is horizontal and changes curvature at the critical point.
−RTcr/(vcr−b)2 + 2a/vcr3 = 0 ... (1)First derivative of P = RT/(v−b) − a/v2.
2RTcr/(vcr−b)3 − 6a/vcr4 = 0 ... (2)Second derivative.
Divide (2) by (1): 2/(vcr − b) = 3/vcr ⇒ vcr = 3bEliminates a and T.
Put in (1): RTcr/(4b2) = 2a/(27b3) ⇒ a = 27RTcrb/8
Pcr = RTcr/(2b) − a/(9b2) = RTcr/(8b) ⇒ b = RTcr/(8Pcr)Put v = 3b into the vdW equation itself.
a = 27R2Tcr2/(64Pcr)Substitute b into a = 27RTcrb/8.
Other equations of state (2018 4b, 2022 1d, 2023 1d)
  • Redlich-Kwong: P = RT/(v − b) − a/[v(v + b)√T], a = 0.42748R2Tcr2.5/Pcr, b = 0.08664RTcr/Pcr.
  • Soave-Redlich-Kwong: P = RT/(v − b) − aα/[v(v + b)], a = 0.42748R2Tcr2/Pcr, b as RK, α = [1 + m(1 − √TR)]2, m = 0.480 + 1.574ω − 0.176ω2 (ω = acentric factor; N2: 0.039).
  • Virial equation: Z = Pv/RT = 1 + B(T)/v + C(T)/v2 + ... B, C are virial coefficients (functions of T only) found from experiment or molecular theory. Use: at low density keep only B (two-term form); the more terms kept, the higher the density for which it is accurate. It has a sound theoretical basis (B represents two-molecule interactions, C three-molecule).

A10 Thermodynamic relations: Maxwell relations, expansivity, compressibility, Joule-Thomson Possible · 46%Hard

Past-paper questions · Only if time

  • 2023 Q4(a) [12] Explain the significance of Maxwell relations. How do they allow entropy changes to be found where direct measurement is impossible?
  • 2023 Q4(b) [8] Short notes: (i) volume expansivity, (ii) isothermal compressibility.
  • 2022 Q8(b) [13] What is a Maxwell relation? Why do we need Maxwell relations? Express them in equation form.
  • 2022 Q8(a) [10] "A cooling effect cannot be achieved by throttling unless the fluid is below its maximum inversion temperature": explain.
★ REMEMBER IT
  • Maxwell relations from "Good Physicists Have Studied Under Very Fine Teachers" square (G, p, H, S, U, V, F, T) or just remember the first: (∂T/∂v)s = −(∂p/∂s)v. Joule-Thomson coefficient μ = (∂T/∂p)h: positive → gas cools when throttled.
Before you start: why we need relations between properties

We can measure p, v and T directly, and cp with a calorimeter, but u, h and s cannot be measured. Thermodynamic relations express their changes in terms of measurable quantities. They come from mathematics: for a property z(x, y), dz = M dx + N dy is exact, so (∂M/∂y)x = (∂N/∂x)y.

Maxwell relations (2022 8b, 2023 4a)

Start from the four Gibbs equations (exact differentials of u, h, Helmholtz function a = u − Ts and Gibbs function g = h − Ts):

du = T ds − p dv dh = T ds + v dp da = −s dT − p dv dg = −s dT + v dp

Applying the exactness test to each gives the four Maxwell relations:

(∂T/∂v)s = −(∂p/∂s)v (∂T/∂p)s = (∂v/∂s)p (∂s/∂v)T = (∂p/∂T)v (∂s/∂p)T = −(∂v/∂T)p

Significance: (1) The last two replace entropy derivatives, which cannot be measured, by p-v-T derivatives, which can be measured or taken from an equation of state. (2) They make it possible to build steam and refrigerant tables of u, h, s from p-v-T and cp data. (3) They give general relations for du, dh, ds, cp − cv and the Clapeyron equation. Example of finding Δs without measuring it: ds = (cp/T)dT − (∂v/∂T)pdp; at constant T, Δs = −∫(∂v/∂T)pdp, which for an ideal gas gives −R ln(p2/p1).

Volume expansivity and isothermal compressibility (2023 4b)
  • Volume expansivity (coefficient of volumetric expansion) β = (1/v)(∂v/∂T)p (unit 1/K): fractional change in volume per degree temperature rise at constant pressure. For an ideal gas β = 1/T.
  • Isothermal compressibility κ = −(1/v)(∂v/∂p)T (unit 1/kPa): fractional decrease in volume per unit pressure rise at constant temperature (positive because v falls as p rises). For an ideal gas κ = 1/p; for liquids it is tiny (nearly incompressible).
  • They are measurable and appear in cp − cv = vTβ2/κ.
Throttling and the maximum inversion temperature (2022 8a)

Throttling (valve, porous plug) is a constant-enthalpy process. The Joule-Thomson coefficient μJT = (∂T/∂p)h tells whether the temperature falls: since pressure drops (dp < 0), cooling (dT < 0) needs μJT > 0. Constant-h lines on a T-p diagram rise to a maximum: the locus of these maxima is the inversion line (μJT = 0). To the left of it (lower p) μJT > 0 and throttling cools; to the right it heats. The highest temperature on the inversion line is the maximum inversion temperature. Above it, every constant-h line has μJT < 0, so throttling at any pressure warms the gas. Hence cooling by throttling is possible only below the maximum inversion temperature (that is why H2 and He, whose inversion temperatures are 202 K and 40 K, must be pre-cooled before Joule-Thomson liquefaction).

Memory trick: Maxwell from Gibbs: "T-s and p-v are partners": each relation pairs T with s and p with v, cross-differentiated; the sign is minus when p and T sit on the same side as in "−s dT − p dv".

  • 2020 Q5(a) [10] Write down the advantages of vapour absorption refrigeration over vapour compression refrigeration.
  • 2019 Q7(a) [10] With a neat schematic, describe the working principle of a vapour absorption refrigeration system.
  • 2018 Q6(b) [12] Why is VCR (vapour compression refrigeration) called work-operated and absorption refrigeration heat-operated? With the p-h diagram, describe the VCR mechanism.
  • 2017 Q6(c) [8] Describe the mechanism of a vapour compression refrigeration system with p-h and T-s diagrams.
  • 2017 Q6(d) [10] An ice plant produces 10 tonnes of ice per day at 0 °C from water at 20 °C. Estimate the compressor motor rating if COP (coefficient of performance) = 2.5 and overall electro-mechanical efficiency = 90 %.
★ REMEMBER IT
  • Vapour compression: compressor → condenser → expansion valve → evaporator; COP = (h1 − h4)/(h2 − h1). Absorption: the compressor is replaced by absorber + pump + generator (heat-driven; NH3-water or LiBr-water).
Before you start: how a refrigerator moves heat uphill

A refrigerant boils at a low temperature when its pressure is low. In the evaporator it boils and absorbs heat from the cold space; the vapour is then compressed to a high pressure so that it can condense at a temperature above the room; in the condenser it rejects heat to the surroundings; finally an expansion (throttle) valve drops its pressure again. COP (coefficient of performance) = refrigerating effect/work input.

Ton of refrigeration (TR) = rate of heat removal that freezes 1 short ton of water at 0 °C in 24 h ≈ 211 kJ/min = 3.517 kW.

Vapour compression refrigeration (2017 6c, 2018 6b, 2021 7a)
  1. 1-2 isentropic compression in the compressor: saturated vapour at evaporator pressure → superheated vapour at condenser pressure. win = h2 − h1.
  2. 2-3 constant-pressure heat rejection in the condenser: vapour → saturated liquid. qH = h2 − h3.
  3. 3-4 throttling in the expansion valve: h4 = h3 (vertical line on p-h); pressure and temperature drop, some liquid flashes to vapour.
  4. 4-1 constant-pressure heat absorption in the evaporator: the mixture evaporates taking heat from the refrigerated space. qL = h1 − h4.

COPR = qL/win = (h1 − h4)/(h2 − h1)

Advantages of VCR: high COP; compact, small size for a given capacity; temperature of the evaporator can be adjusted easily; low running cost where electricity is available. Disadvantages: needs high-grade energy (electricity) to drive the compressor; compressor is noisy, has many moving parts and needs maintenance; refrigerant leakage (some refrigerants harm the ozone layer or cause global warming).

Work-operated vs heat-operated (2018 6b): VCR is called work-operated because the refrigerant vapour is raised to the condenser pressure by mechanical work in a compressor. An absorption system is heat-operated because the compressor is replaced by an absorber-pump-generator set in which the pressure rise is achieved mainly by supplying heat to the generator; the pump work for liquid is negligible.

Vapour absorption refrigeration: ammonia-water (2019 7a, 2022 6b)
  1. Condenser, expansion valve and evaporator work exactly as in VCR, with ammonia (NH3) as refrigerant and water as absorbent.
  2. Ammonia vapour leaving the evaporator enters the absorber, where it dissolves in weak aqua-ammonia solution. The dissolving releases heat, which is removed by cooling water (low temperature helps absorption).
  3. The strong solution (rich in NH3) is pumped by a small liquid pump to the generator pressure (little work because liquid is pumped).
  4. In the generator, heat from a low-grade source (steam, waste heat, solar, gas flame) drives ammonia vapour out of the solution. A rectifier removes water vapour so only dry ammonia goes to the condenser.
  5. The weak solution returns from the generator to the absorber through a pressure-reducing valve, passing a regenerator (heat exchanger) that preheats the strong solution and cools the weak solution.
  6. Ammonia vapour condenses in the condenser, is throttled and evaporates in the evaporator, producing the refrigeration effect.
Advantages of VAR (vapour absorption refrigeration) over VCR (2020 5a) and comparison (2023 7a)
Vapour compression (VCR)Vapour absorption (VAR)
Driven by mechanical work (compressor, electricity)Driven by heat (generator): waste heat, steam, solar, gas
Compressor: noisy, many moving parts, wearOnly a small pump moves: quiet, little wear, long life
High COP (2-5)Low COP (0.3-1.2)
Performance falls at part load; liquid refrigerant may damage the compressorWorks well at part load; no damage from liquid in the evaporator outlet
Compact, lower capital cost for small unitsBulky, higher capital cost, but cheap to run where waste heat exists
Refrigerants: R-134a, R-410A, ammoniaPairs: NH3-water, water-LiBr

Advantages of VAR: uses low-grade or waste energy instead of electricity; few moving parts, so quiet and low maintenance; no lubrication problem; capacity is easily controlled by the generator heat input; not damaged by liquid refrigerant leaving the evaporator.

Numerical: ice plant motor rating (2017 6d)
Step (write this)Why / what it means
Heat removed per kg of water: q = cw(20 − 0) + hif = 4.187 × 20 + 335 = 418.74 kJ/kgCool water to 0 °C (sensible) and freeze it (latent heat of fusion 335 kJ/kg).
Q̇L = 10,000 × 418.74/(24 × 3600) = 48.47 kW (≈ 13.8 TR (ton of refrigeration (3.5 kW)))10 tonnes = 10,000 kg per day.
Ẇ = Q̇L/COP = 48.47/2.5 = 19.39 kWCompressor shaft power.
Motor rating = 19.39/0.90 = 21.5 kWDivide by the electro-mechanical efficiency.

Memory trick: VCR order "Com-Con-Ex-Ev". VAR replaces the compressor with "A-P-G": Absorber, Pump, Generator (plus rectifier and heat exchanger).

B1 Power cycle basics: air-standard assumptions, gas vs vapour cycles, Carnot cycle Very likely · 100%Easy

Past-paper questions · Next to add

  • 2020 Q4(a) [8] What is a power cycle? How does the Carnot efficiency vary with boiler and condenser pressure?
  • 2020 Q4(b) [4] Why is the Carnot cycle not used in practice?
  • 2019 Q6(a) [8] What is an air-standard cycle? Write down the air-standard assumptions.
  • 2019 Q5(a) [8] What is mean temperature of heat addition? Show that cycle efficiency is a function of it.
  • 2018 Q5(a) [7] What is an air-standard cycle? Write down the air-standard assumptions of an actual cycle.
  • 2018 Q6(a) [5] Write down the basic differences between gas power cycles and vapour cycles. Why is the Carnot vapour power cycle not used in practice?
  • 2017 Q5(c) [4] What is air-standard cycle efficiency? (Diesel derivation part in B4.)
★ REMEMBER IT
  • Air-standard assumptions: air is the working fluid in a closed loop, ideal gas; combustion is replaced by heat addition from outside; exhaust by heat rejection; all processes internally reversible. Cold-air-standard: also constant cp, cv at 25 °C.
Before you start: what a power cycle is

A power cycle is a repeated series of processes in which a working fluid takes heat from a hot source, produces net work, rejects heat to a sink and returns to its starting state. Car engines, gas turbines and steam power plants all run on power cycles. A refrigeration cycle runs the other way: it takes work and moves heat from cold to hot.

Real cycles are complicated (combustion, friction, changing composition), so we analyse idealised cycles that keep the main features but are simple enough to calculate.

Classification of thermodynamic cycles (2023 5a)
  • Power cycles (produce work) vs refrigeration / heat pump cycles (consume work).
  • Gas cycles: working fluid stays a gas throughout (Otto, Diesel, Dual, Brayton, Stirling, Ericsson). Vapour cycles: fluid changes between liquid and vapour (Rankine, vapour-compression refrigeration).
  • Closed cycles: the same fluid is returned to the start (steam plant, closed gas turbine). Open cycles: fresh fluid enters each cycle and exhaust leaves (car engine, open gas turbine).
  • Internal combustion (fuel burnt inside the system: petrol and diesel engines, gas turbines) vs external combustion (heat supplied from outside through a boiler or heat exchanger: steam plant, Stirling engine).
Air-standard cycle and air-standard assumptions (2018, 2019, 2021, 2022)

An air-standard cycle is the idealised model of a gas power cycle (IC engine or gas turbine) in which the working fluid is taken as air undergoing a closed cycle. Its efficiency is called the air-standard efficiency (2017 5c): η = wnet/qin of that ideal cycle, which depends only on ratios such as r and γ.

  1. The working fluid is air, which circulates continuously in a closed loop and always behaves as an ideal gas.
  2. All processes making up the cycle are internally reversible.
  3. The combustion process is replaced by a heat-addition process from an external source.
  4. The exhaust process is replaced by a heat-rejection process that restores the fluid to its initial state.
  5. Cold-air-standard assumption (extra): specific heats are constant at their room-temperature (25 °C) values: cp = 1.005, cv = 0.718 kJ/kg K, γ = 1.4.
Gas power cycles vs vapour cycles (2018 6a, 2021 5a)
Gas power cycleVapour power cycle
Working fluid stays gas (air / combustion gases)Fluid changes phase (water ↔ steam)
Heat added and rejected with changing temperatureMost heat added and rejected at constant temperature (boiling, condensing)
Compression of gas needs large work: back work ratio 40-80 %Liquid is pumped: pump work only 1-2 % of turbine work
Usually internal combustion, open cycle (engines, gas turbines)External combustion, closed cycle (steam plant)
Examples: Otto, Diesel, Dual, BraytonExamples: Rankine, Carnot vapour cycle
Carnot cycle (2023 5a)
  1. 1-2 reversible isothermal heat addition at TH: gas expands slowly, taking QH from the source.
  2. 2-3 reversible adiabatic (isentropic) expansion: temperature falls from TH to TL, work is produced.
  3. 3-4 reversible isothermal heat rejection at TL: gas is compressed, giving QL to the sink.
  4. 4-1 reversible adiabatic compression: temperature rises back to TH.

On T-s it is a rectangle: QH = TH(s2 − s1), QL = TL(s2 − s1), so η = 1 − TL/TH, the highest efficiency possible between the two temperatures.

Why the Carnot (vapour) cycle is not used in practice (2018 6a, 2020 4b):

  1. Isothermal heat addition is possible only inside the wet dome, so TH is limited to the critical temperature (374 °C for water), which keeps the efficiency low.
  2. The turbine would have to expand steam of low quality: water droplets erode the blades.
  3. Compression ends at saturated liquid starting from a wet mixture: a compressor cannot handle a two-phase mixture, and stopping condensation exactly at the right quality is impossible to control.
  4. Isothermal processes need very slow heat transfer (huge surface or very long time), and the net work per cycle is small compared with the size of the machine.
Mean temperature of heat addition (2019 5a, 2020 4a)
Step (write this)Why / what it means
In the Rankine cycle heat is added from 2 to 3 at varying temperature. Define Tm such that qin = Tm(s3 − s2).The area under 2-3 on T-s equals the area of a rectangle of height Tm.
Tm = (h3 − h2)/(s3 − s2)For constant-pressure heat addition q = h3 − h2.
Heat is rejected at constant T0 (condenser): qout = T0(s3 − s2)Condensation is isothermal.
η = 1 − qout/qin = 1 − T0/TmSo efficiency rises when Tm rises or T0 falls.

Effect of boiler and condenser pressure: raising the boiler pressure raises Tsat and so Tm → higher η (but more moisture at turbine exit). Lowering the condenser pressure lowers T0 → higher η (limited by the cooling-water temperature and air leakage). The same reasoning applies to the Carnot efficiency 1 − TL/TH, with TH = Tsat(pboiler) and TL = Tsat(pcondenser).

Memory trick: Air-standard assumptions = "A-R-C-E": Air ideal gas in a closed loop, Reversible, Combustion → heat in, Exhaust → heat out (+ Cold = constant cp). Carnot = "T-S-T-S": isoThermal, isentropic, isoThermal, isentropic.

LEARN IT FROM ZERO
Psychrometry, from zero

Air always carries invisible water vapour. Warm air can hold more than cold air. Relative humidity φ says how full the air is compared with the most it could hold at that temperature (pv/ps). Specific humidity ω says how many kg of water per kg of dry air: ω = 0.622 pv/(p − pv). Cool air without changing ω and φ rises until it hits 100 %: that temperature is the dew point, where water starts to condense (cold glass sweating).

The enthalpy per kg of dry air is h = 1.005t + ω(2501 + 1.88t) kJ/kg: the first part warms the dry air, the second evaporates and warms the water. Put any temperature and RH (relative humidity) into the calculator; the graph below is a mini psychrometric chart.

Interactive calculator (needs JavaScript; open the HTML version).

Interactive graph (needs JavaScript; open the HTML version).

Before you start: psychrometry = the study of moist air

Air always carries some water vapour. Psychrometry is the study of the properties of air-water vapour mixtures, used in air conditioning, drying and cooling towers. Atmospheric air is treated as a mixture of dry air and water vapour, both ideal gases; by Dalton, p = pa + pv.

Steam table value needed: the saturation pressure ps at a temperature (e.g. 30 °C → 0.04247 bar). All formulas below use pv and ps in the same unit as p (bar here).

Definitions (2017 7b, 2018 8a, 2020 6b, 2021 8b, 2023 8a)
  • Dry air: air with no water vapour. Moist air: mixture of dry air and water vapour. Saturated air: moist air holding the maximum vapour possible at its temperature (pv = ps).
  • Dry-bulb temperature (DBT): temperature of the air measured by an ordinary thermometer, unaffected by moisture.
  • Wet-bulb temperature (WBT): temperature shown by a thermometer whose bulb is covered by a wet wick with air flowing over it; evaporation cools it below DBT.
  • Wet-bulb depression: DBT − WBT; zero for saturated air.
  • Dew point temperature (DPT): temperature at which water vapour starts to condense when moist air is cooled at constant pressure: Tsat at pv.
  • Specific humidity (humidity ratio, absolute humidity) ω: mass of water vapour per kg of dry air: ω = mv/ma (kg/kg dry air).
  • Relative humidity φ: ratio of the actual vapour mass to the maximum the air could hold at the same temperature: φ = mv/mg = pv/ps.
  • Degree of saturation μ: ω/ωs, the ratio of the actual specific humidity to that of saturated air at the same DBT.
  • Psychrometry (psychrometrics): the science of the thermodynamic properties of moist air and its processes.
Everyday questions

Why is DBT always greater than WBT? (2019 8a) At the wet bulb, water evaporates into the passing air; the latent heat of evaporation is taken from the bulb, so it cools below the air temperature. Evaporation stops only when the air is saturated (φ = 100 %), and then WBT = DBT. Since air is never more than saturated, DBT ≥ WBT.

Why does a wet cloth dry faster in winter than in summer? (2017 7a, 2019 8b) Drying depends on the difference between the vapour pressure at the cloth surface and pv of the air, i.e. on the relative humidity. In Bangladesh the summer (monsoon) air is hot but very humid (φ 80-95 %), so it can take little extra vapour and drying is slow. Winter air is dry (low φ, large wet-bulb depression), so evaporation is fast. (In a climate where summer is dry, the opposite would hold: the answer is about humidity, not temperature alone.)

Why do we feel sweaty in summer and dry in winter? (2018 8b) The body cools by evaporating sweat. In humid summer air, φ is high, so sweat evaporates slowly and stays on the skin: we feel sticky and sweaty. In winter the air is dry (low pv), moisture evaporates quickly from the skin and lips, so they feel dry.

Derivation: specific humidity (2017 7c)
Step (write this)Why / what it means
ω = mv/maDefinition.
mv = pvV/(RvT), ma = paV/(RaT)Both are ideal gases occupying the same V at the same T (Dalton).
ω = (Ra/Rv)(pv/pa) = (0.287/0.4615)(pv/pa)Ra = 8.314/28.97, Rv = 8.314/18.015.
ω = 0.622 pv/(p − pv)pa = p − pv, with p the barometric pressure. So ω depends only on the vapour pressure and the barometric pressure.
Derivation: degree of saturation (2023 8b) and φ = μ/[1 − (1 − μ)ps/p] (2019 8c)
Step (write this)Why / what it means
ω = 0.622pv/(p − pv), ωs = 0.622ps/(p − ps)Saturated air at the same DBT has pv = ps.
μ = ω/ωs = (pv/ps) · (p − ps)/(p − pv) = φ(p − ps)/(p − pv)Degree of saturation expressed with pressures; since ps > pv, μ < φ slightly.
Put pv = φps: μ(p − φps) = φ(p − ps)Remove pv.
μp = φ(p − ps + μps) = φ[p − (1 − μ)ps]Collect the φ terms.
φ = μ/[1 − (1 − μ)(ps/p)]Divide by p.
Adiabatic saturation: enthalpy stays constant (2018 8c)
Step (write this)Why / what it means
Unsaturated air (state 1: T1, ω1) flows over water in a long insulated channel and leaves saturated (state 2: T2, ω2 = ωs). Make-up water at T2 is added at the rate it evaporates.Set-up: steady flow, adiabatic, no work.
Mass of dry air: ṁa1 = ṁa2 = ṁa; water: ṁaω1 + ṁw = ṁaω2 ⇒ ṁw = ṁa(ω2 − ω1)Mass balances.
Energy: ṁah1 + ṁwhf2 = ṁah2, h per kg dry airSFEE (steady-flow energy equation) with Q = W = 0.
h1 + (ω2 − ω1)hf2 = h2Divide by ṁa.
The term (ω2 − ω1)hf2 is very small (ω difference ~0.01 × hf ~100 kJ/kg ≈ 1 kJ/kg)Make-up water enthalpy is negligible.
h1 ≈ h2: the enthalpy of moist air is (practically) constant; the process follows a constant-WBT line on the chartSensible heat lost by the air = latent heat gained by the vapour. T2 is the adiabatic saturation temperature ≈ WBT.
Psychrometric chart (2023 8c) and cooling with dehumidification (2021 8a)
  • Horizontal axis: dry-bulb temperature; vertical lines are constant DBT.
  • Vertical axis (right): specific humidity ω; horizontal lines are constant ω and also constant dew point (read DPT (dew-point temperature) where the horizontal line meets the saturation curve).
  • Saturation curve (φ = 100 %) on the left, with curved constant-φ lines (10 %, 20 %, ...) below it.
  • Constant WBT lines slope down to the right, nearly parallel to constant enthalpy lines (enthalpy scale on the left edge).
  • Constant specific-volume lines are steeper sloping lines (m3/kg dry air).

Cooling and dehumidification: air at state 1 is cooled at constant ω (horizontal line to the left): ω stays the same while φ rises, until it reaches the saturation curve at the dew point. Further cooling condenses water: the state moves down along the saturation curve, so ω decreases (water is removed) and φ stays at 100 %. Finally the air is usually reheated at constant ω to a comfortable temperature, which lowers φ to 40-60 %.

Carrier’s equation (used in every numerical)

pv = pwb − (p − pwb)(tdb − twb)/(1544 − 1.44 twb)

pwb = saturation pressure at the WBT, t in °C. Then ω = 0.622pv/(p − pv), φ = pv/ps, μ = ω/ωs, DPT = Tsat(pv), h = 1.005t + ω(2500 + 1.88t) kJ/kg dry air, v = RaT/(p − pv).

1. DBT 35 °C, WBT 31 °C, 1.0132 bar (2019 8d)
Step (write this)Why / what it means
pwb (31 °C) = 0.04496 bar; ps (35 °C) = 0.05628 barSteam table.
(i) pv = 0.04496 − (0.96824 × 4)/(1544 − 44.64) = 0.04496 − 0.00258 = 0.0424 barCarrier.
(ii) ω = 0.622 × 0.0424/(1.0132 − 0.0424) = 0.0272 kg/kg dry air
(iii) φ = 0.0424/0.05628 = 75.3 %
(iv) DPT = Tsat(0.0424 bar) = 30.0 °CInterpolate in the saturation table.
(v) h = 1.005 × 35 + 0.0272(2500 + 1.88 × 35) = 35.2 + 69.8 = 104.9 kJ/kg dry air
(vi) v = 0.287 × 308.15/(101.32 − 4.24) = 0.911 m3/kg dry airVolume per kg of dry air: dry air at its own partial pressure (kPa).

Interactive calculator (needs JavaScript; open the HTML version).

Before you start: what a gas mixture problem asks

Air, natural gas and combustion products are mixtures of gases. If each component is an ideal gas, the mixture is an ideal gas too, with its own molar mass and gas constant. The whole topic is one chain: masses → moles → mole fractions → apparent molar mass → gas constant → volume and density → specific heats.

Moles: n = m/M (kmol). M: N2 28, O2 32, CO2 44, CH4 16, CO 28 kg/kmol. Ru = 8.314 kJ/kmol K.

Definitions (2019 7b, 2021 7d, 2022 7b)
  • Gas mixture: a physical combination of two or more gases that do not react; each component keeps its own properties (air = N2 + O2 + Ar + ...).
  • Gravimetric analysis: composition given by the mass of each component: mass fraction mfi = mi/mm, Σmfi = 1.
  • Volumetric (molar) analysis: composition given by the number of moles (or partial volume) of each component: mole fraction yi = ni/nm; for ideal gases volume fraction = mole fraction.
  • Ideal gas: a gas obeying Pv = RT (no intermolecular forces, negligible molecular volume).
  • Partial pressure: the pressure a component would exert if it alone occupied the whole volume at the mixture temperature: pi = yip.
Dalton and Amagat (2019 7c, 2020 6a, 2021 7b, 2022 7b)
  • Dalton’s law of additive pressures: the pressure of a gas mixture equals the sum of the pressures each gas would exert if it existed alone at the mixture temperature and volume: pm = Σpi(Tm, Vm).
  • Amagat’s law of additive volumes: the volume of a gas mixture equals the sum of the volumes each gas would occupy if it existed alone at the mixture temperature and pressure: Vm = ΣVi(Tm, pm).
Derivations (2017 8c, 2019 7c, 2018 7a)
Step (write this)Why / what it means
Each component alone in V at T: piV = niRuT; the mixture: pV = nRuTIdeal gas law for the component and for the mixture.
Divide: pi/p = ni/n = yi ⇒ pi = yipPartial pressure = mole fraction × total pressure.
Add over all components: Σpi = (Σni)RuT/V = nRuT/V = p(i) Dalton’s law follows, since Σni = n.
Σyi = Σni/n = n/n = 1(ii) Sum of mole fractions.
m = Σmi = ΣniMi; Mm = m/n = Σ(ni/n)Mi = ΣyiMiApparent molar mass (2018 7a).
Rm = Ru/Mm = ΣmfiRi(iii) Gas constant of the mixture.

Apparent molar mass (2017 8b): Mm = mtotal/ntotal = ΣyiMi: the mass of one kmol of the mixture. No molecule has this mass; it is only an average (air: 28.97, but every molecule is either N2 of 28 or O2 of 32, etc.).

Mixture specific heats

cp,m = Σmficp,i, cv,m = cp,m − Rm. If only γ is given: cp,i = γiRi/(γi − 1). With γ N2 = 1.40, R = 0.2968: cp = 1.039; CO2 γ = 1.29, R = 0.1889: cp = 0.8405 kJ/kg K.

LEARN IT FROM ZERO
Otto, Diesel and Dual, from zero

All three cycles squeeze air (1→2, isentropic), add heat (2→3), let it push the piston (3→4, isentropic) and dump heat at constant volume (4→1). The only difference is how the heat is added: Otto (petrol) all at constant volume (a sudden spark explosion), Diesel at constant pressure (fuel sprayed in while the piston moves), Dual partly each.

Efficiency rises with compression ratio r. For the same r, Otto > Dual > Diesel, because Diesel's heat goes in while the gas is already expanding (cut-off ratio rc > 1 costs efficiency). But diesels run at r = 14–22 while petrol engines are knock-limited to 8–11, so in practice the diesel is more efficient. Use the graph.
