Before you start: how a reciprocating engine works

A piston moves inside a cylinder between the top dead centre (TDC), where the volume is smallest (the clearance volume), and the bottom dead centre (BDC), where it is largest. The distance between them is the stroke, and the volume swept is the displacement volume. Compression ratio r = Vmax/Vmin = VBDC (bottom dead centre)/VTDC (top dead centre).

Petrol (spark-ignition) engines are modelled by the Otto cycle (heat added at constant volume), diesel (compression-ignition) engines by the Diesel cycle (heat added at constant pressure), and real high-speed diesel engines by the Dual cycle (part at constant volume, part at constant pressure). Mean effective pressure MEP = wnet/(vmax − vmin): the constant pressure that would give the same net work over one stroke.

Cycles on p-v and T-s (2017 5a)

Mark qin on the heat-addition line and qout on the rejection line; the enclosed area on p-v is wnet and on T-s it is qnet = wnet.

Four-stroke Otto (spark-ignition) engine (2023 7b)
  1. Intake (suction) stroke: piston moves TDC → BDC with the intake valve open; fuel-air mixture is drawn in.
  2. Compression stroke: both valves closed; piston moves BDC → TDC compressing the mixture (ideal 1-2). Just before TDC the spark plug fires.
  3. Power (expansion) stroke: combustion raises the pressure almost at constant volume (ideal 2-3); high-pressure gases push the piston to BDC (ideal 3-4), producing work.
  4. Exhaust stroke: exhaust valve opens (ideal heat rejection 4-1); piston moves BDC → TDC pushing out the burnt gases.
  5. One power stroke per two crankshaft revolutions.
Otto cycle efficiency
Step (write this)Why / what it means
qin = cv(T3 − T2), qout = cv(T4 − T1)Constant-volume processes.
η = 1 − (T4 − T1)/(T3 − T2)
T2/T1 = rγ−1 = T3/T4 ⇒ T4/T1 = T3/T2Isentropic processes between the same volumes.
ηOtto = 1 − T1/T2 = 1 − 1/rγ−1Depends only on r.
Diesel cycle efficiency in terms of r and rc (2017 5c)

Misprint: the 2017 paper says "pressure ratio"; for the Diesel cycle it must be the cut-off ratio rc = v3/v2.

Step (write this)Why / what it means
qin = cp(T3 − T2), qout = cv(T4 − T1)2-3 at constant p, 4-1 at constant v.
η = 1 − (T4 − T1)/[γ(T3 − T2)]γ = cp/cv.
T2 = T1rγ−11-2 isentropic.
T3 = T2rc = T1rcrγ−12-3 constant p: T ∝ v.
T4 = T3(v3/v4)γ−1 = T3(rc/r)γ−1 = T1rcγ3-4 isentropic, v4 = v1, v3/v1 = rc/r.
η = 1 − T1(rcγ − 1)/[γT1rγ−1(rc − 1)]Substitute; T1 cancels.
ηDiesel = 1 − (1/rγ−1) · (rcγ − 1)/[γ(rc − 1)]

Diesel less efficient than Otto for the same r (2019 6b): the bracket (rcγ − 1)/[γ(rc − 1)] is always greater than 1 for rc > 1 (e.g. rc = 2: (2.639 − 1)/1.4 = 1.17). So the Diesel efficiency subtracts a larger quantity from 1 than Otto does: ηDiesel < ηOtto, and the gap grows with rc (more fuel). As rc → 1 they become equal.

Dual (limited-pressure) cycle (2018 5b, 2021 5b)

Why "limited pressure": in a real high-speed CI engine, part of the fuel burns almost instantly (at nearly constant volume) and the rest burns while the piston moves (at nearly constant pressure). The constant-pressure part limits the peak cylinder pressure to what the engine structure can stand, hence "limited pressure cycle".

Efficiency with pressure ratio rp = p3/p2 and cut-off ratio rc = v4/v3:

ηDual = 1 − (1/rγ−1) · (rprcγ − 1)/[(rp − 1) + γrp(rc − 1)]

Setting rc = 1 gives the Otto formula, and rp = 1 gives the Diesel formula: so the Dual cycle lies between them.

Comparison: same compression ratio and same heat rejection (2021 5b, 2018 5b)
Step (write this)Why / what it means
All three share state 1, state 2 (same r) and the heat-rejection line 4-1, so qout is the same area under 4-1.Same starting point and same rejection.
On T-s, a constant-volume line is steeper than a constant-pressure line (dT/ds = T/cv > T/cp).Explains why the Otto heat addition curve lies highest.
Heat added = area under the heat-addition curve from s2 to s4: largest for Otto, then Dual, then Diesel: qin,Otto > qin,Dual > qin,Diesel.
η = 1 − qout/qin with equal qout ⇒ ηOtto > ηDual > ηDieselWhy: Otto adds its heat at the highest mean temperature.
For the same maximum pressure and temperature (a fair practical comparison) the order reverses: ηDiesel > ηDual > ηOtto, because the Diesel engine can use a much higher compression ratio.

Diesel or petrol: which runs at a higher compression ratio? (2022 7a) Diesel engines (r = 14-22, vs 7-12 for petrol). In a petrol engine the fuel-air mixture is compressed; too high a ratio makes it self-ignite early (knock / detonation), which damages the engine, so r is limited. A diesel engine compresses only air and needs the air hot enough (above the fuel’s auto-ignition temperature) to ignite the injected fuel, so it requires a high r and has no knock limit; this is also why diesel engines are more efficient.

Before you start: the Rankine numerical recipe

State 1 (pump inlet): saturated liquid at the condenser pressure: h1 = hf, v1 = vf. Pump: wp = v1(p2 − p1), h2 = h1 + wp. State 3 (turbine inlet): read h3, s3 from the superheated table at p and T. State 4: s4 = s3; x4 = (s4 − sf)/sfg; h4 = hf + x4hfg. Then η = [(h3 − h4) − wp]/(h3 − h2).

Keep pressure in kPa in the pump formula: m3/kg × kPa = kJ/kg.

★ REMEMBER IT
  • Raise Rankine efficiency: raise the average temperature of heat addition (higher boiler pressure, superheat, reheat, regeneration) or lower the condenser pressure. Reheat also keeps the turbine exit dryer (quality > 0.9).
Before you start: the steam power plant in one picture

A steam power plant has four parts: a pump raises the pressure of water, a boiler turns it into high-pressure superheated steam, a turbine expands the steam to produce work, and a condenser turns the low-pressure steam back to water. The ideal model is the Rankine cycle.

Two numbers decide everything: the average temperature at which heat is added (higher is better) and the temperature at which heat is rejected (lower is better). Every improvement method moves one of them.

Ideal Rankine cycle (2017 6a)
  1. 1-2 isentropic compression in the pump: saturated liquid at the condenser pressure is pumped to the boiler pressure. wp = h2 − h1 = v1(p2 − p1).
  2. 2-3 constant-pressure heat addition in the boiler: compressed liquid → saturated → superheated vapour. qin = h3 − h2.
  3. 3-4 isentropic expansion in the turbine to the condenser pressure. wt = h3 − h4.
  4. 4-1 constant-pressure heat rejection in the condenser to saturated liquid. qout = h4 − h1.

ηth = wnet/qin = [(h3 − h4) − (h2 − h1)]/(h3 − h2) = 1 − (h4 − h1)/(h3 − h2)

h-s (Mollier) diagram: the same cycle drawn with h vertical: 3-4 is a vertical line (isentropic) whose length is the turbine work, 1-2 is a tiny vertical line (pump work), and 2-3 and 4-1 follow constant-pressure lines. It is convenient because the work and heat appear directly as vertical distances.

Actual vs ideal Rankine cycle (2019 5b)
  • Fluid friction: pressure drops in the boiler, condenser and pipes, so the pump must deliver a higher pressure and the turbine receives a lower pressure.
  • Heat loss to the surroundings from steam pipes and turbine, so more heat must be supplied in the boiler.
  • Irreversibilities in the pump and turbine: entropy rises, so 1-2a and 3-4a slope to the right. ηP = (h2s − h1)/(h2a − h1), ηT = (h3 − h4a)/(h3 − h4s).
  • Subcooling of the condensate below saturation (to avoid cavitation in the pump).
How to increase the efficiency of the Rankine cycle (2022 5a, 2023 5b)
  1. Lower the condenser pressure (lower Tout): the extra net work is the shaded strip at the bottom of the T-s diagram. Limit: Tsat must stay above the cooling-water temperature (≈ 10 °C above); side effects: air leakage into the condenser and higher moisture at the turbine exit.
  2. Superheat the steam to a higher temperature (raises Tm,in): more work and less moisture at turbine exit. Limit: metallurgy, about 620 °C.
  3. Raise the boiler pressure (raises Tsat and Tm,in): more efficient, but for a fixed turbine inlet temperature the exit moisture increases; this is solved by reheating. Modern supercritical plants run above 22.06 MPa.
  4. Reheat the steam between turbine stages, and regeneration (feedwater heating with bled steam): see below.
Why superheat? Why reheat? (2019 5c, 2021 6a, 2017 6b)

Superheating raises the mean temperature of heat addition (higher η), increases the work per kg, and keeps the steam drier at the turbine exit so blades are not eroded (quality should stay above about 0.9).

Reheat cycle: steam expands in the high-pressure turbine to an intermediate pressure, returns to the boiler to be reheated (usually to the same temperature), and then expands in the low-pressure turbine. qin = (h3 − h2) + (h5 − h4), wt = (h3 − h4) + (h5 − h6).

When recommended: when a high boiler pressure is used to gain efficiency and the exit moisture would otherwise exceed about 10-12 %. Optimum reheat pressure: about one quarter to one fifth of the boiler pressure. Lower reheat pressure gives drier exit steam but heat is added at a lower average temperature (efficiency may fall); higher reheat pressure adds little. In practice it is chosen to keep the exit quality at the limit (as in the 2021/2023 numerical), and single reheat raises efficiency by about 4-5 %.

Regeneration and cogeneration (2022 5b, 2021 6b)

Why regeneration: in the simple cycle the feedwater enters the boiler cold (state 2), so heat is added at a low temperature, which lowers Tm. Bleeding some steam from the turbine to heat the feedwater raises the temperature at which boiler heat starts, so η increases. It also de-aerates the water (open heater) and reduces the volume of steam the last turbine stages and condenser must handle.

Cogeneration: production of more than one useful form of energy (e.g. electricity and process heat/steam) from the same energy source; the waste heat of the power cycle is used for a process instead of being rejected, so the utilisation factor (useful work + useful heat)/fuel energy can reach 80-90 %.

Open FWH (feedwater heater) working (2021 6b): after the low-pressure pump (1-2), feedwater enters a mixing chamber (open FWH) where it mixes with a fraction y of steam bled from the turbine at the heater pressure (state 6). The mixture leaves as saturated liquid at the heater pressure (state 3), and a second pump raises it to the boiler pressure (3-4). For 1 kg through the boiler, (1 − y) kg goes through the condenser.

Derivation: efficiency of the ideal regenerative cycle (2023 6a, 12 marks)
Step (write this)Why / what it means
Mass balance on the open FWH (per kg of steam through the boiler): y kg bled at state 6, (1 − y) kg feedwater at state 2, 1 kg out at state 3.Choose 1 kg at the boiler as the basis.
Energy balance (adiabatic, no work): y h6 + (1 − y)h2 = h3 ⇒ y = (h3 − h2)/(h6 − h2)Energy in = energy out for the mixing chamber.
qin = h5 − h4Boiler heats 1 kg from state 4 to state 5.
qout = (1 − y)(h7 − h1)Only (1 − y) kg reaches the condenser.
wt = (h5 − h6) + (1 − y)(h6 − h7); wp = (1 − y)(h2 − h1) + (h4 − h3)1 kg expands to the bleed pressure; (1 − y) kg continues. Two pumps.
η = (wt − wp)/qin = 1 − (1 − y)(h7 − h1)/(h5 − h4)Equivalent forms. Compared with the simple cycle, qin falls more than wnet, so η rises.
Open vs closed feedwater heaters (2023 6b)
Open FWH (direct contact)Closed FWH (surface type)
Bled steam and feedwater mix directlyHeat transferred through tubes, streams do not mix
Both streams at the same pressure; outlet is saturated liquid at heater pressureStreams can be at different pressures; feedwater may stay at boiler pressure
Needs a pump after each heaterNeeds no extra pump per heater (drain is trapped back or pumped forward)
Simple, cheap, good heat transfer, also de-aerates the waterMore complex and costly (tube bundle), lower heat transfer (terminal temperature difference)
Feedwater leaves at the saturation temperature of the heaterFeedwater leaves slightly below the bled-steam saturation temperature

Memory trick: Rankine improvements: "Low C, High S, High B, Re-Re" = Lower Condenser pressure, Higher Superheat, Higher Boiler pressure, REheat, REgeneration. Bleed fraction: "y = rise needed / rise available" = (h3 − h2)/(h6 − h2).

★ REMEMBER IT
  • Brayton: η = 1 − 1/rp(γ−1)/γ; write x = rp0.2857 once; T2 = T1x, T4 = T3/x.
Before you start: the gas turbine

A gas turbine has a compressor, a combustion chamber and a turbine on one shaft. Air is compressed, fuel is burned at constant pressure, and the hot gases expand through the turbine, which drives the compressor and produces net power. The ideal model is the Brayton cycle.

Back work ratio rbw = wcompressor/wturbine: in gas turbines it is large (40-80 %), so component efficiencies matter a lot.

ηBrayton = 1 − 1/rp(γ−1)/γ T2s/T1 = T3/T4s = rp(γ−1)/γ

1. Ideal Brayton: rp = 8, 300 K, 1300 K (2023 6c)
Step (write this)Why / what it means
rp0.2857 = 80.2857 = 1.811Cold-air-standard, γ = 1.4.
T2 = 300 × 1.811 = 543.4 K; T4 = 1300/1.811 = 717.7 K(i) Exit temperatures.
η = 1 − 1/1.811 = 44.8 %(ii) With Cengel’s air tables (variable cp): 544.3 K, 770.1 K, 42.6 %.
2. Actual Brayton: ηC = 80 %, ηT = 85 % (2021 5c)
Step (write this)Why / what it means
T2a = T1 + (T2s − T1)/ηC = 300 + 243.4/0.80 = 604.3 KCompressor needs more work than ideal.
T4a = T3 − ηT(T3 − T4s) = 1300 − 0.85 × 582.3 = 805.0 K(i) Turbine gives less work than ideal.
wc = 1.005 × 304.3 = 305.8; wt = 1.005 × 495.0 = 497.5 kJ/kg
(ii) rbw = 305.8/497.5 = 0.61561.5 % of the turbine work drives the compressor.
qin = 1.005(1300 − 604.3) = 699.2; (iii) η = (497.5 − 305.8)/699.2 = 27.4 %Cengel Example 9-6 with air tables: 598 K, 853 K, 0.592, 26.6 %.
3. Brayton between 101 and 505 kPa, 300-1200 K (2022 6c)
Step (write this)Why / what it means
rp = 505/101 = 5; 50.2857 = 1.584
T2 = 300 × 1.584 = 475.1 K; T4 = 1200/1.584 = 757.7 K
(i) η = 1 − 1/1.584 = 36.9 %
(ii) wc = 1.005(475.1 − 300) = 176.0 kJ/kg
(iii) wt = 1.005(1200 − 757.7) = 444.5 kJ/kgNet work 268.5 kJ/kg; check: 268.5/(1.005 × 724.9) = 36.9 %.

Memory trick: Brayton = "one number, one formula": everything comes from rp0.2857. Multiply T1 by it, divide T3 by it.
